course.title: Acute abdomen
course.html:
= group of syndromes with rapid, severe (lethal if untreated) acute evolution, triggered by virtually any organ into abdomen

  • Term emphasizes how prompt surgeons’ diagnostic and therapeutic response must be to prevent patient’s death
  • Not every acute abdomen requires surgery (sometimes even contraindicated)

Main types

Peritonitic- Peritonitis (localized or diffuse)
- Acute appendicitis
- Diverticulitis etc.
Obstructive- All variants of acute nonvascular bowel obstructions
Hemorrhagic- Ruptured ectopic pregnancy or hemorrhagic ovarian cyst
IschemicIschemic- Mesenterial infarctions
- Fallopian tubes’ torsion

Diagnosis (anamnesis) → Pain is dominant!

Onset- Abrupt → perforated peptic ulcer, fallopian tube torsion, acute mesenteric artery
obstruction
- Progressive → acute appendicitis, cholecystitis
Location, migration,
radiation		- Location of pain corresponds to abdominal wall projection of underlying organ
(somatic pain)
- Initial pain may differ from one during examination (migration)
- Epigastric pain: liver (left lobe), biliary, acute pancreatic disease
- Hypogastric pain: uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, urinary bladder, distal ureters
Typical radiations
- Renal colic (nonsurgical abdominal emergency) - pain radiates from lumbar location
along abdominal topographic projection to hypogastric region and genitals
- Ovarian/ fallopian tube - pain radiates cranially
- Acute cholecystitis or subphrenic abscess - pain radiates up to right shoulder
(diaphragmatic irritation)
- Ectopic ruptured pregnancy or ruptured spleen - pain radiates to left shoulder
Continuous/
intermittent		- Septic intra- or retroperitoneal conditions generate intense and continuous pain
(typically perforated peptic ulcer)
- Same continuous pain but more intense by ischemic emergencies (bowel infarction,
fallopian torsion, bowel torsion, strangulated hernias, acute pancreatitis)
- Intermittent, colicky pain → initial phases of nonvascular acute bowel obstructions
- After 6-12 hours abdominal distension becomes dominant, while colicky pain’s
intensity and frequency diminishes due to bowels’ muscular layers exhaustion
Intensity of pain,
aggravating and
relieving factors		- Intense pain - organ perforations or ruptures → peritonitis
- Even more intense - acute ischemia (abrupt, brutal onset, shocking intensity, cold
sweating, no respond to painkillers, decreases after 10-12 h due to total destruction of
bowl including nerves (delusive lull = delayed diagnosis and treatment !)
- Pat. are agitated, restless (necrotic pancreatitis, ischemic conditions, renal colic)
- Pat. with diffuse peritonitis are still, motionsless, scarcely breathing
  • Anorexia, nausea, vomiting - always associated
  • Typical for acute appendicitis (first anorexia, then pain, nausea and vomiting follow after)
  • In acute pancreatitis repeated vomiting does not relief nausea
  • Proximal small bowel obstruction → vomiting frequent, with clear bile
  • Lower obstructions → vomiting rarer, voluminous and turbid
  • Distal small bowel obstructions especially 12-24h after onset → vomitus is voluminous and fecaloid
  • Bowel movements - reflex reaction to any peritoneal injury (localized or diffuse, chemical or purulent peritonitis,

bowel or other abdominal organ ischemia or perforations, hemoperitoneum, acute pancreatitis, etc.)

  • Conditions that cause bowel paresis but are to a surgical acute abdomen → surgery is prohibited in such cases !!!
  • Abrupt, brutal liver failure
  • Severe ascites in cirrhotic pat.
  • Acute diabetic ketoacidosis
  • Severe uremia
  • Severe electrolyte imbalance (especially hypoK)
  • Severe asthma attacks
  • Acute and prolonged urinary retention
  • Hip fractures
  • Acute basal pneumonia; pleural effusions
  • ATTENTION: sometimes paradoxical acceleration of bowel peristalsis → irritation diarrhea
  • partial, lateral bowel strangulations, small femoral or obturator hernias, long- lasting unrecognized diffuse or

localized peritonitis

  • Fever
  • a) Non-perforated acute appendicitis: starts sub-febrility (37.3-37.8ºC), but when appendicular gangrene,

perforation or abscess develops → fever will climb up to 38.5-39.5ºC

  • same happens in all similar abdominal conditions
  • b) Paradoxically normal body temperature in immuno-suppressed patients (AIDS, advanced disseminated cancers,

DM, aged, patients under chemotherapy or chronic corticoids treatment)

  • Past medical history, age, gender, previous surgeries
    • Appendectomy in young female → suspicion of right fallopian or ovary condition
    • Cholecystectomy in female patient → acute cholangitis, acute pancreatitis due to remnants
    • Surgery for acute obstructions → suspicion for bowel adhesions
    • Female pat. with dark colored genital bleedings, delayed menstruation → ectopic pregnancy
    • Most frequent causes in young males - acute appendicitis and hernias
    • Most frequent cause in young females - rupture of graafian follicle or hematic ovarian cyst
    • In male adults - perforated peptic ulcer, acute pancreatitis due to alcohol
    • In adult females - pelvic inflammatory disease, acute lithiasic cholecystitis and ectopic pregnancy

Physical exam

Inspection- Altered respiration due to pain
- Abdominal distension may be impressive
- Post-OP surgical scars
- Hernias
- Ask pat. to show you where pain is
Auscultation- “noisy abdomen” with colicky pain → initial phase of acute obstruction
- In late phases over 12-24h bowel paresis can occur “silent abdomen”
- Most severe condition (bowel infarction) has very early paresis
Palpation- Start away from pain, gentle, observe reaction
- Localized or diffused tenderness
- Muscle rigidity
- Rebound tenderness
- “jarring test” - outstanding accuracy in detecting localized peritoneal inflammation
(patient is asked to jump abruptly on his/her heels after rising on his/her toes;
provoked pain is localized accurately on abdominal wall projection of underlying
inflamed viscus)
Percussion- May be very painful
- May confirm bowel distension, ascitic fluid, inflammation, tumoral mass
DRE→ Mandatory!
+ Vaginal exam in females

book.html:
The acute abdomen – general aspects

Doru Munteanu

Although widespread and generally accepted, the term “acute abdomen”, adjoining these two words, seems not entirely correct from the semantic point of view. But surgery is straight and precise and so are surgical terms. Thus in just two words, the term “acute abdomen” covers a group of syndromes with rapid, severe (lethal if untreated) acute evolution, triggered by virtually any organ contained into the abdomen. A separated category of acute abdominal conditions do not require surgical intervention (which, on the contrary, might be harmful); sometimes, the clinical distinction between the two is difficult and engages the clinicians’ responsibility. On the other hand, the term emphasizes how prompt surgeons’ diagnostic and therapeutic response must be in order to prevent patient’s death.

The main types of SAA are:

  • Peritonitic - (peritonitis – localized or diffuse - , acute appendicitis,

diverticulitis, etc.)

  • Obstructive - (all variants of acute nonvascular bowel obstructions)
  • Haemorrhagic – (ruptured ectopic pregnancy or hemorrhagic ovarian

cyst)

  • Ischaemic – (mesenterial infarctions, fallopian tubes’ torsion)

I.A correct diagnosis requires a thorough anamnesis.

Among all symptoms, pain is dominant, being the patient’s most frequent reason to appeal to medical care; it presents various features that need to be fast and correct recognized.

Some important semiologic features must be correctly interpreted: onset, localization, intensity, continuous/intermittent, spread, aggravating/relieving circumstances, duration, etc.

The onset, for example, might be abrupt (perforated peptic ulcer, fallopian tube torsion, acute mesenteric artery obstruction) or progressive (acute appendicitis, cholecystitis).

Location, migration, extension and radiation of the pain offer important clues. Very often, location of pain corresponds to the abdominal wall projection of the underlying organ (somatic pain); nevertheless, initial location of pain might differ from the one the patient describes during the examination (in acute appendicitis pain is initially epigastric but several hours later it migrates in the right lower quadrant). On the other hand, in a peptic ulcer perforation, pain is initially epigastric as well, but the intensity is much higher; in small anterior duodenal perforations, sometimes one can follow the dispersion of the gastric content, following the extension of the pain from the epigastric region (initial location) to the right, below the liver (right upper quadrant), then to the right parietocolic gutter, into the right lower quadrant before it becomes diffuse (according to the diffusion of the spilled gastroduodenal content and concomitant extension of the peritoneal irritation/inflammation). Epigastric pain can be generated by liver (left lobe), biliary, or pancreatic acute conditions as well. Hipogastric located pain usually orientates the clinician’s attention towards uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, urinary bladder, distal urethers. As for radiation of the pain, here are several typical examples: - during a renal colic (a nonsurgical variant of abdominal emergency), pain radiates caudally from the lumbar initial location along the uretheral abdominal topographic projection, to the hypogastric region and genitals, while ovarian/fallopian tube generated pain, radiates cranially, upstream the same route; – in an acute colecystitis or subphrenic abcess, pain radiates up to the right shoulder (diaphragmatic irritation) while in ectopic ruptured pregnancy or ruptured spleen, pain radiates to the left shoulder.

Continuous/intermittent: septic intra- or retroperitoneal conditions usually generate intense and continuous pain (the classic example of diffuse peritonitis resulting from a perforated peptic ulcer); the same continuous pain, yet much more intense, is generated by ischaemic abdominal emergencies (acute bowel infarction, fallopian tube torsion, bowel torsion, strangulated hernias, or an acute pancreatitis). Intermittent, colicky pain, defines the initial phases of nonvascular acute bowel obstructions, being generated by intense peristaltic contractions; after 6-12 hours however, abdominal distension becomes dominant, while colicky pain’s intensity and frequency diminishes, due to bowels’ muscular layers exhaustion.

Intensity of pain, aggravating and relieving circumstances:Intense

pain is generated usually by organs’ perforations or ruptures, with subsequent abrupt contamination of the peritoneal cavity. Yet some conditions do generate even more intense pain, up to the level of “excruciating”, and these are the ones generated by acute ischaemia, i.e., the acute mesenteric obstruction with consequent acute bowel ischaemia and infarction; not only this condition generates one of the most intense pains described, but it represents the most lethal abdominal condition. The pain, initially located periumbilically, has an abrupt, brutal onset (especially in mesenteric acute embolism), with extreme, shocking intensity, is continuous, does not respond to pain-killers, the patient is livid (pallor associated with cyanosis) and covered with cold sweating.Even here, though, after 10-12 hours, the intensity of pain diminishes significantly, due to two concomitant mechanisms: first, the endogenous endorphins and second, the irreversible and total ischaemic necrosis of the bowel’s structures – including the nervous ones-; Thus, paradoxically (and clinically delusive!), paralleling the patient’s abdominal and general aggravation, the severity of pain may diminish (delusive lull = delayed diagnosis and treatment !). Sometimes the current crisis is preceded by several episodes of “abdominal angina” (intermittent but incomplete, reversible attacks of mesenteric ischaemia during meals).

Patients with severe necrotic acute pancreatitis and those with abdominal ischaemic conditions are agitated, restless, cannot stand still (but so are the ones with reno-uretheral colick !), while the ones with diffuse peritonitis are still, motionless, scarcely breathing, as even the slightest movement aggravates their pain.

Anorexia, nausea, vomiting: are always associated with the acute abdominal conditions. Anorexia is typically associated to acute appendicitis, preceding or being concomitant with the pain, while nausea and vomiting usually follow. In acute pancreatitis, repeated vomiting does not relieve nausea. In acute bowel obstructions there are some semiologic features of vomiting and vomitus which correctly interpreted, are very important for a proper evaluation of the patient; thus, in proximal small bowel obstructions, vomiting is frequently repeated, the vomitus contains clear bile; in lower situated obstructions, the vomiting becomes rarer, but the vomitus becomes progressively voluminous and turbid, while in distal (terminal ileon-situated) small bowel obstructions, especially 12-24 hours after the onset of obstruction, vomitus is voluminous and fecaloid(bad prognosis sign!).

Bowel movements: in the vast majority of the cases, do accurately reflect the severity of abdominal acute conditions, as seizing of bowel peristalsisalways occurs as a reflex reaction to any peritoneal injury (localized or diffuse, chemical or purulent peritonitis,bowels’ or other abdominal organs’ ischaemia or perforations, haemoperitoneum, acute pancreatitis, etc.). Nevertheless, a long list of other conditions do frequently generate bowel pareses (but are never to be erroneously included among the SAA conditions): abrupt, brutal liver failure with acute, high volume formation of ascites in liver cirrhotic patients, acute diabetic acido-ketosis, severe uremia, severe electrolytic imbalances (hypokalemia especially), severe asthmatic attacks, acute and prolonged urinary retention, hip fractures, acute basal pneumonia, pleural effusions, etc. In all these conditions, surgery is strongly prohibited !

On the other hand, rarely, severe intra-abdominal conditions may evolve not with as expected, bowel paresis, but, on the contrary, with a paradoxical acceleration of bowels’peristalsis, generating a so-called “irritation diarrhoea” (partial, lateral bowel strangulations – small femoral or obturatory hernias!-, long-lasting, unrecognized, neglected, diffuse or localized peritonitis); in these cases, the absence of the “no bowel movements” sign, may erroneously delay surgical treatment, with catastrophic results !

Fever is another clinical parameter which needs to be correctly interpreted; basically, all inflammatory, septic and ischaemic intra-abdominal conditions are associated with alterations of the body’s temperature. For example, a typical, non-perforated acute appendicitis, always evolves with sub-febrility (37.3-37.8ºC); hours or days later however, when the appendicular gangrene, perforation or abscess develops, fever will climb up to 38.5-39.5ºC. The same happens in all similar abdominal conditions; yet, there are again, some particular cases with severe abdominal surgical emergencies, but with paradoxicaly normal body temperature (immunosuppressed patients-AIDS-, advanced disseminated cancers, diabetes mellitus, aged, patients under chemotherapy or chronic corticoids treatment); especially in aged patients, shivers might be the clinical correspondent to fever; actually, in these above-mentioned categories of patients, not only fever, but all the other clinical signs and symptoms are frequently incomplete or mild, below the usual threshold of recognition.

Apart from the above-mentioned data, a good anamnesis also provides important information concerning age, gender, medical history; all these data, corroborated with the previously obtained ones, may help a lot in completing patients’diagnostic puzzle. For example,the most frequent causes of SAA in young male adults are acute appendicitis and hernias, while in young females, rupture of a graafian follicle or of a hematic ovarian cyst. In male adults, perforated peptic ulcer,acute pancreatitis due to alcohol consumption and acute appendicitis; in adult female patients, pelvic inflammatory disease, acute lithiasic cholecystitis and ectopic pregnancy.

Similar previous episodes (biliary colicks, acute pancreatitis, peptic ulcer), may facilitate identification of the current episode, as well as any available information concerning patient’s medical history. Hence, previous surgical procedures, help us exclude some of the potential causes of SAA (previous “ectomies”, such as appendectomy, cholecystectomy, female reproductive system operations, etc.); ● a previous appendectomy in a young female patient with right lower quadrant pain, facilitates a faster diagnostic orientation directly towards a rightfallopian or ovarian acute condition (however, in female patients with particularly long leftfallopian tubes and consequently mobile left ovaries, left ruptured haematic cysts have been identified and operated in the right iliac fosa). Three more special mentions must be made: ● a cholecystectomy in the recent history of a female patient presenting with abdominal pain, fever, shivers, jaundice and vomiting, especially if there is available data concerning the number and dimensions of the gallbladder stones (multiple small stones, for example), helps in establishing only on clinical bases, a strong suspicion of an acute cholangitis, acute pancreatitis, due to, probably remnant main bile duct lithiasis (a much worse variant might suspect a iatrogenic biliary injury as well);● Previous surgery, especially pelvic procedures, in patients with acute bowel obstruction, makes us suspect obstructive adhesions, easy to manage surgically; ● young adult female patient with recent history (one-two months) of irregular, dark-colored genital bleedings, delayed menstrual cycle and hypogastric pain with bilateral lumbar irradiation, must be immediately suspected of ectopic pregnancy (a severe, potentially lethal haemorrhagic abdominal surgical emergency) with imminence of fallopian tube rupture, and promptly treated accordingly.

II. General physical examination.

So far, anamnesis has offered us a lot of important information; we’ve already established some strong suspicions without even touching the patient (as a matter of fact, usually anamnesis is taken concomitant with the first steps of the physical examination, which has to be very accurate,thorough, systematic and repeated). After an initial brief but careful general evaluation (in order to exclude from the very beginning immediate life-threatening conditions, i.e. acute anaemia, hypovolemic shock, acute myocardial infarction, deep dehydration, etc. – cases in which prompt resuscitative measures are taken - ), a thorough general examination is done.

Abdominal careful examination is done using the following steps inspection, auscultation, palpation and percussion, followed by rectal examination (in male and female patients) and female genital examination.

  • Inspection:- with the patient in supine position, the abdomen is completely

exposed; respiratory mobility, appearance, postoperatory scars, all these aspects can provide important informations. In a peritonitic type SAA, the respiratory mobility of the abdomen is abolished, every respiratory movement, even a superficial one, generates intense pain; the patient lays still, stiff, rigid; abdominal distension may be impressive in long standing large bowel obstructions; postoperatory abdominal scars may orientate as well; at this point, hernias, primary or incisional, are identified; the patient is asked to indicate with his own hand the abdominal region where pain is maximal. ● Auscultation of the abdomen may reveal normal intestinal sounds; a “noisy”abdomen, with strong, intense and frequent bowel sounds, correlated with abdominal colicky pain, is strongly suggestive for the initial phases of an acute bowel obstruction (OIA); on the contrary, in late phases – over 1224 hours – a bowel paresis occurs and no bowel sounds are heared; Yet, the most severe condition of them all, the bowel infarction, generates from the very beginning a persistent and total bowel paresis, classically described as “the death silence”; in these cases, the patient’s general condition is already severely altered. Well tolerated, important abdominal distensions with temporary bowel sounds abolishment are described in the so-called paralytic ileus-es, generated by extra-abdominal general disturbances. ● Palpation has to be gently, mild; it always has to start away from the area described as painful by the patient, making a permanent comparison between the right and left sides and being careful to patient’s reaction to our maneuvers. If tolerated, gradually deeper palpation follows; in SAA conditions, localized or diffuse abdominal wall point tenderness is the clinical sign that reveals an underlying inflammatory process with consequent peritoneal irritation; usually point tenderness and abdominal muscles’ rigidity is associated with another important clinical sign, the rebound tenderness; again we draw attention on exceptions, cases with paradoxical reactions (or better said, lack of reactions), in which underlying very severe abdominal acute conditions do not generate the expected reaction of the abdominal wall structures! A so called “jarring test” has been described as outstanding accurate in detecting a localized peritoneal inflammatory condition: patient is asked to jump abruptly on his/her heels after rising on his/her toes; the consequently provoked pain is localized accurately on the abdominal wall projection of the underlying inflamed viscus. ● Percussion is very painful in patients with SAA; it may confirm bowel distension, the presence of ascetic fluid or identify abdominal inflammatory or tumiral masses. ●Rectal examination in male patients, rectal and ●pelvic examination in female patients are mandatory.

If the thorough examination was doubtful, never leave the patient; keep him/her under observation and reexamine later. Calling for a colleague’s second opinion is recommended as well.
